description: Join my team and let's explore the space through story telling
summary: Explorer Spirit is a talking robot guide that answers children’s questions about what humans left behind on the Moon and Mars. Kids pick the Moon, Mars, or Explore More, then type or speak a question in any of nine languages. Explorer Spirit finds the answer in NASA’s Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon, Mars landing hardware records, and NASA’s image library. It then tells the answer as a short story in a friendly robot voice, and every answer shows where it came from. The challenge asks for storytelling about discarded equipment. We turned a 22-page NASA catalogue into a conversation that a 10-year-old enjoys. Golf balls, a falcon feather, rovers, parachutes and even bags of astronaut waste become doorways to science, history and the question of how we should treat other worlds. The app is live, free and works in a phone browser with no download or sign-up.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Explorer Spirit is a talking robot guide that answers children's questions about the objects humans left on the Moon and Mars, and about everything a curious child asks next.

•         Three worlds. Moon (objects left on the Moon), Mars (hardware on Mars) and Explore More (any space question). Each opens with its own greeting.

•         Ask by typing or talking, in any of nine languages: English, Indonesian, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic and Hindi. The page opens in the child's device language.

•         Answers come from data first. The app holds NASA's Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon (799 entries), a list of 17 human-made objects on Mars, 13 astronaut topics and 20 space-science topics. It adds real photos from the NASA Image and Video Library and Mars rover facts from the NASA Open API.

•         Every answer shows its source (Aggregate Data, NASA Image Library, NASA Open API). When no curated data matches, the answer is labeled AI General Knowledge. If Explorer Spirit is not sure, it says so instead of guessing.

•         The mascot reacts. It talks with a moving mouth, shows a "?" bubble while thinking, lights a bulb when it finds the answer, and twirls when it gets bored.

How a question is answered:

1.       The child asks a question in the web app.

2.       A serverless function on Netlify searches our structured data with keyword matching. Kid words are mapped to catalogue terms, for example "poop" to "Defecation Collection Device". Questions in other languages are first turned into English keywords so they still match the NASA data.

3.       The matching facts go to Google Gemini Flash-Lite with strict rules: use the NASA facts first, keep every number exact, write for a 10-year-old, never invent a source, and label the basis of the answer. Web search is off.

4.       The browser shows the answer with its source label and reads it aloud with the device's built-in voice.

What benefits does it have?

•         Turns a dry list into wonder. A 22-page inventory of discarded equipment becomes stories that lead to history, science and engineering.

•         Builds good information habits early. Children see where every fact comes from, and learn that "I don't know yet" is an honest answer.

•         Reaches children who don't read English, through nine languages and voice input and output.

•         Free and easy to use. It runs in a phone or laptop browser, with no download, account, ads or cost for schools.

•         Answers the next question too. It covers astronauts, rockets, satellites, space junk and life on other planets, so curiosity is not cut off after one answer.

What is the intended impact of the project?

•         Spark lasting curiosity about space and STEM, especially in countries like Indonesia where children rarely get to talk to a space expert.

•         Make children think about how humans treat other worlds. Learning that we left 25 bags of waste and whole rovers behind starts a conversation about responsibility, space junk and protecting historic sites.

•         Keep the history of exploration alive. The objects are "abandoned but not forgotten": each one becomes a story about the people who left it.

•         Next steps: add Moon missions after 2012 (Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Artemis), have native speakers review every language, and build a museum kiosk mode and a classroom quiz. Before a public launch for children, we would move to an AI service tier and data-protection setup approved for use with children, and test it with teachers and parents.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

•         Coding languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (app and backend), Python (to convert the NASA catalogue PDF into structured data).

•         Backend and hosting: Node.js serverless functions on Netlify; code on GitHub.

•         AI: Google Gemini API (Flash-Lite), used for answers and translation.

•         NASA APIs: NASA Image and Video Library API, NASA Open APIs (Mars Rover Photos mission manifests).

•         Browser features: Web Speech API (robot voice and microphone), Web Audio API (beep-boop sound), HTML canvas (starfield).

•         Design: inline SVG mascot mouth and icons, Fredoka and Nunito fonts (Google Fonts).

•         Hardware: none beyond an ordinary laptop or phone; the app runs in any modern browser.

•         Development help: Claude (Anthropic), as described under Use of Super Intelligence.

How is your project creative?

•         A character, not a search box. Explorer Spirit has a face, a voice and moods. It thinks with a "?", lights up when it finds the answer and twirls when bored, so children talk to it like a friend.

•         Stories instead of lists. The same catalogue row, "Golf balls (2), Apollo 14", becomes the story of Alan Shepard's Moon golf shot.

•         Kid language mapped to NASA language. Children can ask about "poop" and get the official "Defecation Collection Device" record, explained kindly.

•         Honesty is part of the design. Source labels and an "I don't have that yet" reply show children how trustworthy information works.

•         Born from a real childhood question. We built the friend we wished we had when every space book gave us ten new questions.

•         One page, nine languages. The page switches to the child's language automatically, including right-to-left Arabic.

What factors did your team consider?

•         Accuracy. Answers are grounded in NASA data first, numbers are kept exact, and anything outside the data is clearly labeled. We also checked well-known claims against the source; for example, popular articles say 96 waste bags, but the NASA catalogue lists 25.

•         Child safety and privacy. No accounts, no data saved, no ads, and no images of real children. Sensitive topics, such as astronauts who died, are answered gently and respectfully.

•         Accessibility. Voice input and output for children who cannot read or type well yet. A text-only mode when a device has no voice for that language. Clear help when the microphone does not work in a browser. Reduced motion for children who need it.

•         Speed and cost. Answers had to arrive in under 10 seconds on free hosting, so we chose a fast model and a strict time budget. Everything runs on free tiers.

•         Limits of the data. The NASA Moon catalogue dates from 2012, and parts of the Mars list come from secondary sources. We say this openly and plan to add newer missions.

•         Rules of the challenge. No NASA logos or branding, AI use disclosed, AI-generated media watermarked, and every NASA and partner source listed.
